item.title: Phenomenological Bioethics: What Does It Mean to Die Well?
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Phenomenological Bioethics: What Does It Mean to Die Well?

Medicine alone cannot answer the most human of questions.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Dying is not only a medical event.
  • Modern medicine excels at treating disease but frequently struggles with illness.
  • Asking the right questions to the dying is one of the most profound acts of care.

Co-authored by Mark Shelvock and Daniel Wyzynski

Source: Photo by Vitaly Gariev on Unsplash

In the modern fast-paced world, many of us spend little time consciously thinking about our inevitable deaths until we are directly confronted by them. This existential confrontation can occur through a new diagnosis, a loved one’s health declining, an unexpected tragedy, or perhaps when we put on our favourite hospital drama on TV.

A brief history of death in the Western world

According to historian Philippe Ariès, death was once a communal and intimate event within the Western world. People died at home, surrounded by family, within a web of cultural and/or religious rituals.1 Over the course of the 20th century, however, dying became more medicalized; relocated from the home into hospitals and institutions, and transferred from the hands of families into the hands of healthcare providers. As medical interventions progressed and the ability to keep death at bay grew, the location of care shifted to a place where more invasive interventions could be performed — and now a common request that arises in the hospital is for the medical staff to "do everything" to prevent death.

In North America, and across much of the Western world, many people today have little personal experience with dying or death. Alternatively, movies and TV may have taught them to expect a tranquil death that rarely matches reality. This cultural estrangement has real consequences for individuals, families, healthcare providers, and the health system.

The gap between disease and illness

One of the most important distinctions in end-of-life care is between disease and illness. Disease is objective; the measurable, diagnosable change in the body that a clinician can identify and treat. Illness, on the other hand, is subjective and deeply personal. Illness is the lived experience of being unwell, which may include experiences of fear, fatigue, grief, and a loss of identity or other personal struggles that no medical chart can fully capture.

Modern medicine has become extraordinarily good at treating disease, but far less attentive to illness, and to dying.1,2,3 Yet for the person who has become a “patient”, illness is what often matters the most: what it means, how it feels, and what it does to a person's sense of self, their life story, and the impact it has on the people they love the most.4

Pain follows the same logic. Many clinicians learn early that pain is whatever the experiencing person says it is, and two people with identical diagnoses can suffer in radically different ways. Dying, then, is never simply a medical event. It is a disorienting, multidimensional, and existentially raw time in a person’s life.

What people need

The physician-author Atul Gawande put the problem plainly: people facing serious illness have priorities beyond simply prolonging their lives.2 They want to avoid suffering, remain psychologically present, feel connected to the people they love, and they want to reflect on the sense that their lives have been complete and meaningful. The dominant model of technological medical care, Gawande argued, has frequently failed to meet these needs in the 21st century.

What people need at the end of life is not always more intervention, but more presence, listening, psychosocial supports, and more honest conversations about what really matters. This is where phenomenological bioethics enters; it is not just abstract theory, but a practical human philosophy and orientation towards authentic care.

Phenomenological bioethics: starting with the unique person

Phenomenology is the philosophical study of lived experience, and grapples with what it is like to be a conscious, embodied, mortal, and vulnerable human being. The philosopher Fredrik Svenaeus invites us to start with a unique person’s experience of suffering.

This approach asks clinicians and caregivers alike to sit with questions that no brain scan or blood panel can answer:

  • What does dying mean to this person, and where would they like to die? Who needs to be present here for them? Who do they not want to be present?
  • How does serious illness disrupt the narrative they have constructed about themselves: their identity, roles, and sense of a future?
  • What are the person's core values as they undergo this dying experience, and how can we honour these? What supports need to be in place to honour this person’s values and needs?
  • What would it mean for them to continue meaningfully existing in the world while dying?
  • What does suffering mean to them?
Source: Photo by Pouya Hajiebrahimi on Unsplash

What dying well actually requires

Dying well is not about achieving some idealized exit, or being stoic, entirely peaceful, or free from all fear and suffering. It is about being seen as our own person, dying on our own terms: as a full human being with a history, a body, a web of relationships, and a particular way of making meaning in the world.

These questions are not morbid but generous, and asking them is one of the most profound acts of care available to us.

We also acknowledge that phenomenological bioethics has significant limitations. It is difficult to scale its recommendations when faced with institutional and system-wide limitations; further, existentially informed approaches demand time, humility, and relational skills that constrained budgets and widespread burnout make hard to sustain. Still, it offers what medical treatments cannot supply on their own; a way of approaching dying as a fundamentally human experience, and not merely a set of clinical problems to be managed.

To our readers: the question worth asking now, not at the bedside or in crisis, but here, in the quiet of an ordinary day, is: What might it mean for you to die well, and can you talk about what dying well means to you and your loved ones?

Source: Photo of Daniel Wyzynski // Used with permission.

This article was co-authored with Daniel Wyzynski, a Clinical Ethicist, associate scientist, and adjunct research professor at Western University. Daniel specializes in clinical ethics, complex medical deliberation, mental health ethics, and patient-centred and family-centered care within acute and long-term care settings.

item.title: When Casual Dating Comes With Major Expectations
item.description:
Mating

When Casual Dating Comes With Major Expectations

A new preliminary study reveals the assumptions people bring to situationships.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Situationships involve romantic or sexual intimacy without clearly defined commitment.
  • Women are more likely than men to hope situationships will lead to committed relationships.
  • Although 56% of preliminary study participants hoped for more, only 9% of situationships became relationships.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

A “situationship” is more than a casual hookup, but it’s not exactly a committed relationship, either. While there may be sex, emotional intimacy, and even regular dates, it stops short of an established relationship because the partners involved don’t have a clear or mutually agreed understanding of where things stand.

Situationships appear to be on the rise, but what do we actually know about them from a scientific standpoint? For example, do men and women tend to approach them differently? And do they ever turn into romantic relationships?

New preliminary research offers intriguing insight into the nature of situationships.

A Study of Situationships

In this study, researchers surveyed 390 adults, most of whom were from the United States, United Kingdom, or Canada. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 75 and were asked to report on relationship experiences that “exist between casual dating and committed partnerships” that “typically lack clear labels or commitment.”

They were asked about their history with situationships, including how many they’d had, as well as their motivations for pursuing such arrangements and their expectations around sexual exclusivity. They were also asked to define what a situationship means in their own words.

What It Means to Be in a Situationship

Qualitative analyses indicated that the most common features of a situationship included the following:

  • Lack of commitment
  • No mutually agreed relationship status or labels
  • Behaving in ways that are typical for a romantic relationship
  • Engaging in sexual behavior
  • Expressing attachment, affection, and emotional closeness
  • Uncertainty around the rules, expectations, and boundaries of the connection
  • Lack of clarity around where things are headed
  • Existing between relationship categories
  • Sustained or repeated involvement

What these findings tell us is that most people seem to understand situationships as sexual and intimate connections that feature a lot of relationship-like behaviors, but exist in a very ambiguous and unclear state.

Men’s and Women’s Expectations for Situationships

The results also indicated that men and women differed in terms of how they approached situationships. For example, women were significantly more likely than men to report entering these relationships with the hope that they would eventually develop into a committed partnership. They were also more likely to see long-term romantic potential.

However, women were especially likely to describe situationships as emotionally confusing or characterized by mixed signals. In fact, 77 percent of women compared to 50 percent of men said that situationships involve moments of closeness followed by distance. Likewise, 65 percent of women (vs. 44 percent of men) described situationships as carrying on without really progressing toward anything.

These findings suggest that, on average, men tend to approach situationships more casually, whereas women are more likely to view them as a possible stepping stone to a full-fledged romance.

It’s important to reiterate that these are average (not universal) sex differences. However, whenever people enter a relationship with different expectations, there’s extra potential for disappointment.

Do Situationships Ever Turn Into Relationships?

One of the most striking findings was just how rarely situationships actually turned into romances.

Overall, 56 percent of participants said they had entered a situationship hoping it would later become a relationship. However, just 9 percent of past situationships eventually made the transition.

In other words, if you’re hoping for more from a situationship, odds are that it probably won’t work out, despite the fact that these relationships aren’t necessarily brief and are often recurring. In fact, about 41 percent of past situationships lasted at least seven months, with about one-quarter lasting for a year or longer. Also, half of participants reported that they had returned to a previous situationship at some point.

In short, situationships are often prolonged, recurring connections, even when they aren't progressing toward commitment.

Are People in Situationships Monogamous?

Despite the lack of clear labels and expectations, 55 percent of participants assumed their situationship was sexually exclusive. Moreover, 68 percent of women and 58 percent of men agreed that they would feel betrayed if their situationship partner was seeing other people.

This suggests that just because a relationship is undefined, it doesn’t necessarily mean that people enter it free of expectations. Although some might assume that regular sex, emotional intimacy, and going on dates imply exclusivity or growing commitment, their partners may be interpreting the same behaviors very differently.

Takeaways

As with any study, this one has its limitations. In particular, because it involved an online convenience sample, it’s not clear how representative the findings are of the broader population. Also, all participants reported on different-sex situationships, so we can’t say whether the findings would apply to people in same-sex contexts.

That said, the findings still tell us something important, which is that situationships aren't necessarily problematic because they lack traditional relationship labels. The core tension is that partners often don’t understand or agree upon what their connection really means.

While freedom from labels and expectations is part of the appeal of a situationship, it seems that many are still bringing certain assumptions into them. Further, escalating intimacy doesn’t necessarily signal that each partner sees a progression toward commitment.

item.title: Why Introverts May Be Jolted When You Start Talking to Them
item.description:
Introversion

Why Introverts May Be Jolted When You Start Talking to Them

A sudden conversation can interrupt an active inner dialogue.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Sudden conversation may interrupt an introvert's active inner dialogue, not an idle mind.
  • An introvert's initial "wince" at being approached may be an involuntary context switch, not social rejection.
  • Asking “Do you have a minute?” gives someone time to shift from inner thought to conversation.
Source: RDNE Stock project/Pexels

Have you ever been deep in thought, maybe working through a problem, reflecting on a conversation, or composing a mental draft of something, when someone abruptly appears and launches into a distracting monologue? If you’re an introvert, this is likely a very familiar and often uncomfortable experience.

Such moments may involve a collision between two different forms of default attention, one directed inward, and another suddenly redirected outward toward opportunity for social exchange. As for that discomfort, research increasingly suggests that it’s tied to the experience of being, in effect, forcibly pulled out of an active inner world and pushed (maybe even against your will) through a mental portal into a quite different one.

You Were in the Middle of Something

When an introvert appears to be “doing nothing,” they’re very often doing something (the trees falling in these forests, it turns out, make no sound).

They’re likely engaged in inner speech. But I should clarify. That inner speech, that “little voice inside your head,” is actually one of the most common human experiences for all of us (not just introverts), playing a central role in consciousness, especially connecting language and thought.

Research has indicated that this can be monologal (a single stream of inner speech) or dialogal (not just talking to yourself but with yourself). The dialogal form provides an opportunity to imagine others’ perspectives and prepare for social exchanges. Truly then, it can be like role-playing with yourself.

Inner speech has roles in executive function, cognitive self-regulation, working memory, and moral reasoning (so, pretty important). For a given introvert, inner speech may be extremely active; for others, less so.

The Brain's Default Is Anything but Idle

Neuroscience has given us a framework called the default mode network (DMN) for understanding what’s happening during inner talk. These networked brain regions become active when we’re turned inward, whether remembering, imagining, reflecting, planning, etcetera.

In a landmark 2023 review in Neuron, Vinod Menon synthesized decades of DMN research and proposed that the network’s overarching function is to create an “ongoing internal narrative,” essentially a coherent, dynamic stream of thought that integrates memory, language, and especially “self-referential processing,” a narrative, he argued, which is central to the construction of a sense of self ("I think, therefore I am?").

Research by Knyazev and colleagues offers an intriguing clue. They found that introverts and extraverts showed different patterns of brain activity when thinking positively about themselves and their futures. For introverts, that activity was more pronounced in a region associated with more abstract, evaluative thought, while for extraverts it was more pronounced in a region associated with more concrete, situation-specific thought.

The implication is that introverts may be especially inclined toward an inward, evaluative style of thought, and so describing some of us as walking around having conversations with ourselves is, perhaps, reasonable.

The Interruption Problem

Source: Yan Krukau/Pexels

Now consider what happens when someone initiates a spontaneous conversation with a person in this state. What feels to the other person like a neutral social overture may be experienced by the introvert as an interruption (because it is). Research on cognitive disruption has found that disruptive experiences are associated with more frequent self-talk, perhaps because self-talk helps people interpret unexpected events, regulate their responses, and restore a coherent line of thought. Disruption and inner speech might become entangled because when a line of thought is broken, we may use self-talk to find our way back into it, which becomes pretty difficult when someone has just started another conversation with us.

This helps explain the characteristic introvert wince—that micro-expression of feeling startled, possibly slightly irritated, or likely briefly disoriented. Folks often react to such reactions of mine with, “Are you okay?” Sometimes I feel the need to respond with some combination of “Sorry, I was thinking about something” and “Sorry, sometimes I’m a bit slow-to-warm-up.” The science suggests that the little wince may actually signal a rapid, involuntary context switch from internal processing to external social demand.

The Forecasting Gap

Zelenski and colleagues found that introverts overestimate the negative affect—or unpleasant emotion—they’ll experience when acting extraverted, only to enjoy it more than they had anticipated. Partly, this may be due to that slow-to-warm-up-ness I mentioned before. But their finding raises an interesting possibility in the other direction: Might extraverts underestimate how cognitively disruptive their perfectly friendly social overtures can feel to an introvert who was already quite occupied? After all, what feels to one person like the beginning of a conversation may feel to the other like the interruption of one (alas, conversation may be your default mode, but you just interrupted mine).

Rethinking the Social Contract

Source: cottonbro studio/Pexels

This all suggests we might benefit from a more nuanced awareness and approach. A few principles from the research may help:

Signal before you speak. A brief “Hey, do you have a minute?” gives an introvert’s brain time to complete that involuntary context switch rather than forcing an abrupt transition—the cognitive equivalent of knocking before entering. Of course, you can also send a message ahead to let them know when you’ll be stopping by.

Respect the transition. That initial apparent blankness or flatness may be a transition. (Weird, I was just somewhere else, and now you’re here.) It can take a moment to catch up as our brains reallocate resources from internal to external processing (ah, the sweet validation of a scientific explanation).

Recognize the inner life. When someone looks like they’re doing nothing, they may be thinking deeply. Another way of saying it is that the introvert’s inner dialogue isn’t a bug, but a feature—which, for us, fuels self-awareness and depth of understanding, as well as creativity.

Next time an introvert looks mentally jolted when you start talking, consider the possibility that you may have walked into the middle of a conversation.

item.title: When Did Tracking Our Teenagers Become Normal?
item.description:
Adolescence

When Did Tracking Our Teenagers Become Normal?

As location sharing becomes common, are parents making room for teens to launch?

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Location tracking may ease parental anxiety without building teenagers' independence.
  • Constant monitoring makes it harder for parents to practice letting go.
  • Parents can shift energy from monitoring their child to focusing on who they want to be as loving supporters.

As thousands of Australian teenagers head off to "Schoolies"—a traditional holiday celebrating the end of high school—I imagine plenty of parents are feeling a mixture of pride and apprehension. For many young people, this is their first holiday without parents nearby. An important step toward adulthood.

But something has changed.

Parents no longer have to wonder where their teenagers are. Location-tracking apps allow them to follow their movements throughout the day and night.

A recent media release from Life360 caught my attention. The company reports that 94% of school leavers planning a trip intend to use location sharing, with 74% planning to share their location with a parent.

Of course, this is company-commissioned research linked to their tracking apps. But what struck me was how readily location tracking is becoming an accepted part of parenting teenagers.

Have we reached a point where not tracking them feels like irresponsible parenting?

The Parenting Paradox

A recent article in The Atlantic, titled "The Parents Who Never Stop Tracking Their Kids," explores how location tracking has become commonplace in families, even extending into the college and university years.

In my book The Parenting Paradox, I explore how we've arrived at today's intensive parenting culture, where good parenting increasingly means anticipating risks, monitoring well-being, and stepping in before difficulties arise.

Technology has taken this to another level. We can now keep watch over our children even when they're miles away.

But here's the paradox. The more responsibility we take for managing our children's lives, the harder it becomes to give them space to manage their own lives.

Location sharing may be useful at times, particularly when friends are traveling together. But I wonder what happens when parents become accustomed to always knowing where their teenagers (or indeed younger children) are.

We feel uneasy, check the app, and experience some reassurance. Then another worrying thought arises, and we check again. The more we rely on monitoring to settle our anxiety, the less opportunity we have to give space for our teenagers to grow their capacity to manage themselves.

Are we becoming better at managing our worry, or simply more dependent on monitoring to relieve it?

Learning to Let Go

Knowing where a teenager is doesn't tell us whether they're making wise decisions or developing the judgment they'll need in adult life.

Any opportunity for young adults to travel independently, such as "Schoolies," provides an opportunity for sensible conversations about safety, friendships, and responsibility. We should have good, open communication about arrangements made and how our teen has thought through contingencies. But it's also an opportunity for parents to practice something important: managing our own worries rather than continually investing in managing our children.

Perhaps the question isn't simply whether we can track our teenagers. It's whether we're prepared to let them take another step toward adulthood without feeling we must follow their every move.

And maybe that's a growing-up opportunity for parents, too.

item.title: When Huge Is Not Big Enough
item.description:
Body Image

When Huge Is Not Big Enough

Muscle dysmorphia is a form of BDD that masquerades as physical fitness.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Muscle dysmorphia sometimes persists even when a person is clearly, noticeably muscular.
  • The desire to get bigger and stronger can devolve into an unhealthy cycle of anxiety or compulsive striving.
  • Exaggerated images on social media, along with masculine ideals, can reinforce unrealistic body expectations.
  • In therapy, people can learn to distinguish healthy fitness aspirations from distortions to the self-image.

Fans of the X-Men film franchise, which premiered in the long-ago year of 2000, were treated to the original version of Hugh Jackman’s now-longstanding portrayal of the character Wolverine. Appearing frequently shirtless in the movie, at the time Jackman seemed muscular enough to be super-heroic. He has played Wolverine nine more times in the decades since then, but rather than growing older and more relaxed, Jackman’s physique has seemed to develop in the opposite direction. Bigger, leaner, and more defined, Jackman could stand for an increasingly familiar male ideal.

Source: Image generated by ChatGPT

Like him, many men spend hours in the gym trying to bulk up. They may carefully monitor their diets, timing their protein intake for maximum effect. They may indeed grow larger and more muscular; family, friends, and partners will notice. They may share images of weight-lifting transformations on social media, or even consider anabolic steroids or testosterone injections. Despite it all, some of these men will continue to see themselves as too small, too ill-defined, and not muscular enough.

What Is Muscle Dysmorphia?

This condition is known as muscle dysmorphia, a form of body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) characterized by an unrelenting preoccupation with the idea that one is not muscular or lean enough. Even when a man is objectively well built, he may perceive himself as physically inadequate. It’s not common, but it’s real: a 2025 study of nearly fifteen hundred boys and men between the ages of 15 and 35 (Ganson et al., 2025a) concluded that the disorder likely existed in approximately 2.8% of those surveyed — across demographic groups, not only among weightlifters or athletes. (Indeed, a 2024 study in the Journal of Eating Disorders found higher muscle dysmorphia symptom scores among men who wanted to increase their body weight than among those who wanted to reduce it.)

As I’ve suggested, while physical fitness is usually worth aspiring to, there’s a significant difference between ordinary, healthy fitness and muscle dysmorphia. Even when a man is objectively strong, “cut,” and full of muscles, he may look at himself in the mirror and see only weakness. This preoccupation can then lead to repeated, muscle-seeking behavior, such as checking himself in the mirror, researching new exercise routines, measuring body parts, or seeking new nutritional information. It can also involve excessive weightlifting, spending too much time at the gym, or taking on rigid dietary pursuits that can even become unhealthy or dangerous.

But as all that exercise produces results, it never seems like enough: getting bigger just feeds back into the perception that they still aren’t big enough. And when men with the disorder can’t soothe their anxiety by working out, they can feel real emotional distress, as well. The central characteristic of muscle dysmorphia is being absorbed by the perception that one is not muscular enough; it describes men whose daily routine and sense of self are dependent on the pursuit of muscularity, not those who just don’t like missing a workout (Cooper et al., 2020).

How Masculine Body Ideals and Social Media Relate to Muscle Dysmorphia

These days, muscle dysmorphia is particularly associated with male body-image concerns, although women can experience it as well. As we’ve seen in Hugh Jackman’s transformation, men in popular culture are expected to be physically strong and imposing, with muscles sharply defined and standing out through their clothing. (So many superheroes!) Women face body image concerns as well, of course, but the pressure on women often focuses on losing weight and appearing thin rather than strong. For men, being muscular can stand in for physical attractiveness, competence, or even dominance.

It’s easy to find examples of these masculine norms on social media nowadays; just as in the past, we’ve been treated to male movie stars whose bodies are designed to show off a great deal of time in the gym; adherence to these norms has been associated with the symptoms of muscle dysmorphia (Grunewald et al., 2022). Research by Ganson and colleagues (2025b) supported this, finding that greater exposure to muscle-oriented social media content was associated with higher levels of probable muscle dysmorphia.

Filters, strategic lighting, and increasingly sophisticated photo-editing tools can offer further enhancement to these already extreme physiques, and sometimes the men in these social-media posts use performance-enhancing drugs, which pushes them still further out of the realm of the realistic. Overall, the fitness content on social media can complicate the distinction between healthy exercise and unhealthy physical enhancement. Psychological vulnerabilities may also play a role: in a 2024 study of men attending gyms, Kandemir et al. found that perfectionism helped explain the relationship between vulnerable narcissism and the risk of muscle dysmorphia.

Risks Related to Muscle Dysmorphia

Muscle dysmorphia can be harmful in a number of ways. Training too hard, even through pain, can lead to injuries — some of which can be lasting. Restricting one’s diet can also have serious consequences for one’s health, such as hormonal disruption (meaning reduced production of testosterone, among other things), reduced bone density, and an increase in the risk of fractures or hypotension (Mountjoy et al., 2023).

The obsession with being muscular can take its toll on one’s social life, too, when men seem to prioritize their nutrition or their workout schedules over their partners’ needs. Daily work obligations can be affected when muscle dysmorphia affects one’s ability to concentrate (Cooper et al., 2020).

And of course there are the serious emotional consequences of feeling ashamed of oneself — like depression, anxiety, or self-hatred — because of body-image-related beliefs. Even when a man’s friends seem to admire their discipline or dedication, or comment in positive ways about the change in his physical condition, these would-be compliments can have a paradoxically damaging effect if they spur a man to try even harder to achieve his unrealistic muscular aspirations, or if they make his beliefs seem more reasonable than they are.

Seeking Help

As I’ve noted before, men may be comparatively less likely to seek help for emotion-related problems than women; when the topic is body-image concerns, they may be less likely still. Some may not even believe they have a problem, as the effort to become (and look) strong seems to be valued by their peers and by the culture overall (Brown et al., 2023).

In therapy, however, it is possible to draw a subtle but meaningful distinction between a realistic, healthy body image and a source of compulsive striving. Irrational or distorted cognitions may be examined; other sources of self-worth can be identified. In other words, the effort to become “big” may also have an idiosyncratic meaning to each individual man, and this meaning stands a chance of being explored and identified in the context of the therapeutic relationship. (Medical intervention may become necessary as well, in cases involving potentially harmful medications or nutritional restriction.)

In the end, muscle dysmorphia creates a slippery slope: trying to be big seems to promise better self-esteem, but the effort only results in further, more extreme beliefs about how big one needs to be to achieve those benefits. The only real way out is to grow in a different direction — to learn that feeling good means accepting yourself as you are, and trying to live in a healthy way without wondering what you still need to change.

item.title: 6 Steps You Can Practice Daily to Enhance Gratitude
item.description:
Gratitude

6 Steps You Can Practice Daily to Enhance Gratitude

Gratitude is your superpower.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Gratitude can help reduce stress, improve mood, and increase self-esteem.
  • Gratitude can coexist with hardship; a person can appreciate what works without denying what hurts.
  • Daily practices, including resilience exercises and strengthening one's mental muscle, can increase gratitude.

Growing up, I never understood the hype around the concept of gratitude. I always thought gratitude was a glorified term for being thankful for what’s right in front of you. I’ve learned that gratitude is much more than that. Gratitude is actually your superpower.

It can reduce your stress levels, increase your self-esteem, and shift your attention towards positive experiences. The simple act of being thankful for the smallest thing can cause your body to release “feel-good” chemicals that can improve your mood and motivation.

Living a life filled with gratitude can also help you move forward in life. It allows you to believe that there is a brighter tomorrow despite the difficulties you encounter. Life can be very challenging, and gratitude can help you build a more solid foundation.

6 Steps to Strengthen Your Gratitude Superpower

It can take time to strengthen your gratitude superpower. To help you make it a daily practice, start looking at things differently. Start small, and apply these six steps:

  1. Start with a gratitude mindset. Regardless of your life’s challenges, start every day by thinking about what makes you grateful. Say it out loud, write it in a journal, and/or tell a friend before you start your busy day. This gratitude mindset will change how you think about situations and can strengthen your relationships with people. Before you jump to concerns or criticisms, step back and recognize what you appreciate most.
  2. Be thankful for the non-obvious. Whatever is in your life is there for a reason, and most of the time, the reason is not apparent. Start paying attention to the non-obvious people and things that enhance your life. The reason we have so much gratitude merchandise (journals, pens, mugs, and attire) is that it is there to force us to notice, which is called “forced appreciation.” Notice the things you take for granted, and be more grateful.
  3. Do resilience exercises. Enhancing your gratitude superpower is similar to training your mental muscle or strengthening resilience. To practice this muscle daily, do resilience exercises. Pick three things that you are glad that you can do. They can be simple qualities that you may take for granted, such as waking up in the morning, being able to move your body, and/or being able to think. Make it a priority to practice these things each day, and then congratulate yourself for doing them. Give yourself credit, and remember that you deserve to be happy. These resilience exercises can help you overcome obstacles and be more appreciative.
  4. Balance the bad with gratitude. Gratitude is seldom unconditional. Life often provides you both joy and heartache at the same time. So, practicing gratitude can be complicated. You must acknowledge that you have to balance the negative with the positive; for example, instead of a stroke patient only looking at the parts of the body that are limp, the patient can choose to show gratitude for the parts that do work, while acknowledging the parts that don’t. Recognize that life is messy and practicing gratitude requires balance.
  5. Replace high expectations with appreciation. Expectations and gratitude are inversely proportional. If you have high expectations, strive for perfection, and/or feel entitled, it can lead to a lack of gratitude. Avoid looking at life with a lens of lack. Instead, replace your views of life with abundance and appreciation. Be happy for the small things in life, and thank the people who make your life better.
  6. Mirror appreciation of others. If you’re struggling to find things to be grateful for, surround yourself with people who regularly express gratitude. Watch feel-good videos online of people bringing joy to others, pets being affectionate, and/or children giving a parent a hug. Their feelings of appreciation can be contagious. The brain has mirror neurons, which mirror expressions of others. So if a person or pet shows gratitude, your brain cells mirror their emotions.

November is a month committed to gratitude. Our Thanksgiving holiday is often a favorite because there is no pressure to give gifts. Instead, it’s a time to take a break, enjoy each other’s company, and give thanks. And this season of gratitude makes people feel good. People like to especially thank, acknowledge, and appreciate others this time of year. So as we kick off the holidays, take the opportunity to start enhancing your gratitude superpower.

item.title: Why Kissing Matters More Than You Think During Sex
item.description:
Sex

Why Kissing Matters More Than You Think During Sex

The easiest route to better orgasms is one many couples skip.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Kissing is one of the strongest predictors of satisfying sex, and it is especially tied to orgasm for women.
  • Skipping kisses widen the orgasm gap, while kissing more can lower stress and raise relationship satisfaction.
  • A kiss lasting about six seconds is enough to trigger the bonding effects of oxytocin.
Source: WeVibe / Unsplash

In today’s sexual landscape, we are getting a lot of information about how to supercharge our sex lives. There are Instagram ads for vibrators and other accessories, shelves of toys at our local drugstore, and no end of supplements marketed to anyone whose libido might be waning. But the data tells us that actually our strongest—but most undervalued—predictor of satisfying sex is just good old-fashioned kissing. And this is as true for people hooking up with new partners as it is for those in long-term relationships.

So why has kissing fallen out of fashion?

Researcher Lisa Wade (2017) found that in hook-up culture, people tend to follow the “no kissing during sex” rule to preserve boundaries, ostensibly keeping sex casual and emotionally safe. But that strategy for avoiding feeling too close to a casual partner can have an unintended consequence. Eschewing kissing can, as my own students report, leave them feeling empty afterward. For long-term partners, kissing can be bypassed out of time constraints and a misguided attempt at sexual efficiency. When you are trying to squeeze sex in around busy jobs or parenting, it can be tempting to “jump to the main event.” Meanwhile, both groups can be influenced by porn that emphasizes novel activities like choking over “vanilla” activities like kissing. But the research shows that forgoing kissing to keep sex casual or efficient skips the activity that most reliably predicts it being good, and it’s women who pay the price.

Kissing During Sex Predicts Frequency and Enjoyment

When researchers Busby et al. (2021) set out to quantify the impact of kissing on relationship and sexual satisfaction in long-term relationships, they found that both specific kissing (during the most recent sexual experience) and global kissing (during the last year) were positively associated with their subjects’ perspective on the quality of their sex lives and their overall relationship satisfaction. For women, kissing during sex was positively associated with their ability to orgasm, sexual frequency, and indirectly with sexual satisfaction. Because they were more likely to orgasm, this positive reinforcement made them want to have sex more often, creating a virtuous feedback loop. These findings suggest that kissing shouldn’t be thought of as superfluous, but rather reclassified as foundational to relationship maintenance and a couple’s sexual repertoire.

Why Kissing Is Sexually More Beneficial for Women

While both sexes associate more kissing with a stronger relationship, the orgasm benefits definitely skew toward women. Kissing signals emotional closeness, slows the pace of the encounter, and extends foreplay, all of which raise arousal and make orgasm more likely for women.

This is why Wade’s research into hooking up with an understanding that kissing is off the table sets women at a disadvantage. When researcher Frederick and his team (2017) asked a cross-sample of people if their last sexual encounter led to orgasm, unsurprisingly, 65 percent of heterosexual women answered affirmatively compared to 95 percent of heterosexual men. This is called the orgasm gap. Kissing can help close that gap even for new partners.

How Couples Can Leverage Kissing

In addition to incorporating specific kissing back into sex, pay attention to global kissing. The above studies are correlational, but this study isn’t: Kory Floyd and colleagues (2009) assigned married and cohabiting couples to kiss more for six weeks. Compared with controls, the kissing group had lower stress, lower cholesterol, and higher relationship satisfaction. In a classic “fake it till you make it” framework, starting with increasing kissing can lead to a stronger relationship, rather than waiting for events to unfold the other way around.

Don’t Overthink Your Technique

New research from Christopher Watkins and Milena Rota (2026) found that fantasy and sexual imagination inform the perception of a good kiss rather than technique. And even more important than technique is duration. The Gottmans claim that as long as a kiss lasts at least six seconds, the brain releases oxytocin, which is the bonding hormone that enables all of the above (Brittle, 2014).

So, in our overscheduled, overstimulating world, think about coming back to basics. If your sex life has gone flat, kissing is the easiest place to start because it’s free, you can’t run out, its batteries won’t go dead, and best of all, it brings both people into the moment. That's what great sex is all about.

item.title: How Italians Cured My Loneliness
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

How Italians Cured My Loneliness

Personal Perspective: We can learn to break the habits that keep us isolated.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • People who are lonely might be contributing to their own isolation, without realizing it.
  • Cultures that elevate community over individualism have a lot to teach others.
  • It's never too late to build new ways of being and participating in the world.
Dr. Susan Biali with her Italian friend Vincenza
Source: Susan Biali

A couple of years ago, I’d made the painful decision to leave my marriage, and my beloved dog of 13 years had died. Suddenly, I found myself deeply alone.

The life I had always imagined for myself—a long-term stable marriage and a family nested in community—had never materialized.

One day, though, I realized that there was something that I had dreamed of when I was younger, that suddenly might be possible.

Italy.

I went. And I went again. I discovered a lesser-known town in my favorite area, and an affordable apartment that I could use periodically in the off-season. I committed to going, using airline points, when I had lulls between stretches of speaking engagements.

Because of my youthful obsession with all things Italian, I had studied the language. I’d also had a long-distance Italian boyfriend for a few months in my early 30s.

I brushed up via a language app, and this was the key that opened all doors.

In Canada, I was a solitary woman who had to book appointments to see her busy friends, all of whom had families.

In Italy, I found myself swept up into a large, generous family and their circle of friends, and rarely had enough time to sit and read a book.

The way I learned to live in Italy transformed the way I live at home.

Here's how Italy changed me:

1. I pick up the phone when it rings.

I always thought my phone aversion was due to being an introvert. Even if the name on my screen was a friend, I’d send it to voicemail and text them a little bit later.

In Italy, I discovered the delight of being interrupted.

At least once a day, my friend Vincenza knocked at my door unannounced, calling out my name. My old Canadian self might have pretended not to be home, but I began to associate these unexpected visits with delight. Vincenza usually had a plate of hot pasta or pastries in her arms, or her sister Angela would call to invite me for lunch.

The effect stuck. Today, when a friend or family member calls me, I find myself answering. Sometimes I even call them.

2. I've let go of my plan.

Part of why I wouldn’t answer the phone when it rang was because it wasn’t part of "the plan." I ran a tight ship. Or perhaps not actually that tight, because I was usually already behind on the day’s to-do list. There wasn’t room for an unplanned 15-minute chat with a friend.

In Italy, Angela randomly calls to let me know that they’ll gather in the piazza in 10 minutes “because the sun is so beautiful today.”

An impromptu lunch invitation may stretch into a couple of hours around a table with friends.

When I run into Vincenza’s daughter, Nausica, while out running errands, she often invites me for a spontaneous coffee or aperitivo, or to go to a store around the corner and help her pick out a dress for an event.

In my past life, I believed that because I was doing something (anything) else, the natural answer was, "Sorry, not now."

I’ve learned that unless I absolutely must be doing something else, the best answer is “Sure, why not?”

3. I’m much better at receiving.

If you’ve seen the meme of the hyper-independent woman carrying a clothes washer up the subway steps by herself, that’s me.

I don’t like needing or asking for help. I am, however, a professional helper. Literally. I’m a medical doctor, an executive coach, and a professional speaker/educator. Perhaps most importantly, I’m also the first-born daughter of four.

I will help you with things you didn’t even know you needed help with.

Then there are my Italian friends. They don’t need my help. They don’t seem to even want my help.

They stealthily pay for my aperitivo or pizza, sneaking the waiter money while pretending to use the washroom. I once tried to pay for parking, and my friend wrestled me out of the way so intensely that I hesitate to ever attempt it again.

But what about medical help? Surely, there might be potential for heroics. Nope, they already have a doctor in the family.

The thing is, they seem to just enjoy having me around—without me doing anything other than showing up and eating the food they place in front of me, with great enthusiasm. This seems to be all one needs to do to earn permanently adopted status.

I think that was the ultimate blow that broke the chains of my very North American loneliness. In a “What can you do for me?” world, it’s remarkable to discover a collective of people, all of whom seem to live by the same rules: “You’ll always have a place at my table—just don’t argue when I serve you more pasta.”

item.title: How Professionals May Overlook Intrafamilial Child Torture
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

How Professionals May Overlook Intrafamilial Child Torture

Parents who torture children can defy common expectations.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Intrafamilial child torture (ICT) is severe, prolonged, purposeful and deliberate abuse and neglect.
  • Families who inflict ICT can present in a range of ways and don't conform to a single stereotype.
  • Some perpetrators of ICT also coercively control and torture their adult partners.
Source: Cottonbro / Pexels

Coauthored with Pamela J. Miller, JD., MSW

Intrafamilial child torture (“ICT”) usually involves a combination of physical, sexual, and psychological abuse, and intentional neglect, of a child, that is 1) severe and egregious, 2) prolonged without intervention, and 3) deliberate on the part of the offending parent (Miller, et al, 2021). By definition, ICT occurs within the family context and is perpetrated by someone who is considered a child's family member or caretaker.

ICT is different from most physical abuse, which is episodic and often impulsive. Most physical abuse results from parents losing control and/or accidentally hurting a child more than intended. Part of the harm of ICT is its insidious and all-encompassing nature; the child has few avenues for healthy development.

While ICT is thought to be relatively rare, it's still common enough that anyone who works with children or families over a decade is apt to encounter a child who has been or is being tortured. Often, the professional will mistake the ICT for simple abuse or neglect, and will fail to offer the child meaningful assistance.

Surprising Presentations Often Overlooked

We have each seen more than a few cases of ICT over the course of our professional lives (Miller about 50, Fontes about 15). Many professionals have never heard of ICT. But even when they have, they might mistakenly discard the ICT framework if the case before them doesn’t seem to fit their idea of what ICT looks like. This can have fatal consequences.

Our goal here is to expand professionals’ internal schema of how ICT appears by discussing diverse presentations that we’ve encountered. This is a stand-in until research devises undoubtedly different, more robust, evidence-based typologies. We link descriptions to real cases in the popular media, so readers can learn more.

Pillars of the Community

Parents who torture their children don’t necessarily lead marginal lives. They may be wealthy professionals and appear to be caring and competent in their work lives (Miller et al., 2021). Ruby Franke, a parenting influencer, appears to have tortured her children and eventually pleaded guilty to aggravated child abuse. Larry and Carri Williams were popular at their church before their convictions involving assault on one child and the death by torture of another.

Mother-Driven ICT

While most family violence is committed by men, some ICT involves a female caregiver as the primary perpetrator. Adoptive mother Maribel Loera recently pleaded guilty to second-degree murder, concealment of a body, and multiple counts of severe child abuse, thus avoiding the death penalty. According to media reports, two of her surviving children testified to years of severe violence, including burns, beatings, and a knife attack that left permanent scars. Professionals should be aware that ICT can be driven by female perpetrators.

Substance Abusing Perpetrator

Some child torturers’ lives follow a pattern of abuse and withdrawal from drugs; they could be especially dangerous at any part of this cycle. They may act in extremely harmful ways when “out of their wits” from alcohol, methamphetamines, fentanyl, or other substances. However, while the substances may make episodic violence more intense or more frequent, the substances are not the cause. By definition, ICT is purposeful and deliberate.

While there is plentiful research on the higher prevalence of child abuse and neglect among caregivers who abuse substances, we were unable to find research on child torture specifically. But we’ve both seen drug-addled caretakers who seem to have lost any sense of care or morality and torture a child or children over time, sometimes fatally.

Non-Biological Caregivers

The first study to analyze a large body of ICT cases statistically (Rycus et al. 2026) found that non-biological parents are more likely to be perpetrators of ICT than biological parents. This includes stepparents, biological parents’ romantic partners, adoptive parents, foster parents, and relatives caring for children. The case of Larry and Carri Williams (mentioned above) stands out here, where parents of seven biological children adopted two children from Ethiopia, and the mother tortured the older child, Hana, until she died from malnutrition and hypothermia. While the parents used abusive punishments with their biological children, they apparently tortured only their adopted children.

Domestic Abuser Who Tortures Children and an Adult Partner

Sometimes one partner (usually but not always the man in heterosexual couples) coercively controls and tortures not just one or more children, but also his adult partner. In fact, the abuser’s torture of the children may be aimed at dominating his adult partner.

The abuser’s coercive control over his partner incapacitates her ability to protect the children effectively. She may try to deflect the abuser’s rage towards herself. She may sneak the children food when they are locked in the closet. Adult victims may fail to contact authorities due to a combination of fear that their children will be removed and fear that the abuser will kill them and the children before police arrive.

Vanity Fair reported that when the police came to arrest attorney Joel Steinberg and his girlfriend, Editor Hedda Nussbaum, for the death of their adoptive child, Lisa Steinberg, Nussbaum looked like a boxer who had sustained beatings. Nussbaum had a fractured nose and jaw, nine broken ribs, and gangrenous legs.

Targeted Children vs. All Children

In some ICT cases, the parent(s) abuse all the children (e.g., the Turpins, Nixmary Brown, the family of Elisa Izquierdo). In others, the parents seem to differentiate among the children, targeting those children who are not biologically related (as in Hana Williams), who are the oldest, or who are disabled.

Homeschooling

Many caretakers hide their tortured children from public view by homeschooling or “no- schooling” them. The under-regulation of homeschooling allows caretakers to torture children with no oversight from teachers or school officials who might otherwise make child abuse reports (Bartholet, 2020). In a typical case, the Hart parents removed their six adopted children from public school after reports of suspected child abuse. In several of the cases mentioned here, the caregivers withdrew the children from school, including the Turpin, Franke, and Williams cases.

Parental Mental Illness and Personality Disorders

At first glance, it might seem that anyone who tortures a child is “crazy.” However, research is lacking on the possible diagnoses of caretakers who torture their children. In our experience, ICT is often perpetrated by people who show no outward signs of mental illness. People in an acute psychotic episode might kill their children, perhaps thinking that this will “save” them or because they are suffering from persecutory delusions or postpartum psychosis. However, this filicide would fail to meet the criteria of ICT as a deliberate and prolonged series of acts.

Children in Networks: Cults and Trafficking

Sometimes organized groups participate in children’s torture. These can include cults, along with sex and labor trafficking networks. These networks often include adult family members who inflict or permit the abuse, thus qualifying as ICT. One example is Children of God (now renamed Family International), where children were routinely beaten, whipped, sexually abused, and denied education. Sex trafficking of minors involves physical and psychological torture as well as neglect, thus qualifying as ICT when family members are involved.

Conclusions

Caregivers who torture their children can be of high or low social status; related by blood or not; substance abusing or sober; of any gender; and loving or cruel to other children in the home. They are apt to keep the tortured child hidden from public view, through home or no-schooling, or networks organized around cults or crime. Learn about ICT so you can tune in to signs that children you suspect are abused may be suffering far worse: torture.

item.title: How to Survive the Holidays With "Ignorant" Relatives
item.description:
Family Dynamics

How to Survive the Holidays With "Ignorant" Relatives

What if your “ignorant” relative is simply navigating a different mental map?

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Because one's own opinions feel real, relatives who disagree seem "ignorant" rather than simply different.
  • Listening accurately and looking for the values beneath opinions changes the tone of difficult conversations.
  • Warren Farrell’s book “Role Mate, Soul Mate” offers strategies to sustain love that also work with relatives.

One phrase that changed my life forever is: "The map is not the territory."

There is a reality out there—the territory—but our only way to access it is through the representations of it we create and carry around in our heads. These are our maps. And every human being has a slightly different map. When I say "red," and you imagine red, how can we be certain we're imagining the same hue, tint, etc.? We can't.

So, we arrive at a dining table this holiday season convinced that our opinions simply describe what any reasonable and rational person would see when they looked at the world... the facts... the territory. Naturally, a relative who disagrees with our map must be missing some vital information, or be lacking in the intelligence needed to process that information correctly, or both. We think that they are ignorant; if they only had a map as good as ours, they would agree with us.

In Role Mate to Soul Mate, relationship expert Warren Farrell writes that certainty can close us off to other people’s perspectives. His chapter “From Civil War to Civil Dialogue” offers tools for staying in conversation when disagreements get heated.

Nemesis Visualization

Farrell recommends preparing before the meal. Start with “nemesis visualization”: Picture the relative who interrupts, misunderstands you, or repeats their point more loudly. The goal isn’t to rehearse a fight. It’s to let go of the hope that this time you’ll finally change their mind and choose peace instead.

Alone Power

Another tool is “Alone Power”: the ability, on your own, to help another person feel heard. That doesn’t mean agreeing. It means listening closely enough that the other person can see that you are truly trying to understand them. Holiday dinners put this skill to the test; we may say we want less division, while quietly hoping everyone will come around to our view. First, we need to know how to make other people feel heard.

The Three Cs

Next, think of a few qualities you genuinely respect in that relative and recognize in yourself. Farrell calls attention to three possible points of common ground: caring, curiosity, and courage (the three Cs). You might not share all three, and that’s fine. Choose what resonates with you. Finding one shared quality can make it easier to stay curious about the person beneath the argument.

Hold

When the conversation starts to escalate, notice whether you’re already composing your rebuttal. Silently say “hold” to yourself, and then take a deep breath or recall something beautiful that helps you feel grounded. Try these three steps:

  1. Listen without interrupting.
  2. Reflect back what you heard.
  3. Ask, “Did I get that right or did I miss something?”

Keep checking until the other person feels accurately understood.

Feeling heard often reduces someone’s need to keep arguing, so use the holidays to practice your active listening skills.

Visualizing the Virtue

This is my favorite exercise. Farrell’s premise is that a virtue, pushed to an extreme, can become a vice. The exercise asks you to look for the value inside an opinion that irritates you. In his example, a conservative father and liberal daughter discover shared values beneath their political disagreement, including compassion, equality of opportunity, and self-respect. From there, they can replace proselytizing with a search for mutual solutions.

We don’t have to abandon our convictions or pretend to agree with our relatives; we simply have to become sufficiently curious to inquire why the maps in their heads are so different from the maps in ours. We can ask what matters to them, and if the conversation becomes disrespectful or frustrating, we can set a limit: “I care about you, but I don’t want to keep arguing about this. Let’s talk about something else.”

We have to be the change we want to see in the world. Imagine how much more peaceful the world would be if we all remembered that the map is not the territory. We would waste less time believing that other people are ignorant and spend more time becoming curious about their maps. At the end of the day, everyone just wants to feel heard, seen, respected... loved. Maybe a more harmonious, compassionate, and less polarized world starts at your dining room table this holiday season.

item.title: Is Cheating in Marriage Ever Justified?
item.description:
Infidelity

Is Cheating in Marriage Ever Justified?

The deepest damage of infidelity isn't the affair—it's the loss of trust.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Cheating is not only an ethically flawed form of validation; it also injures ourselves.
  • Trust in a relationship is like air. You don’t think about air unless you don’t have it.
  • It’s very simple: If you can’t continue your commitment, tell them rather than going down the road of pretend.

“Yes, cheating can damage a marriage,” a couples therapist I interviewed a few years ago told me, “yet it can also make the marriage stronger.”

This approach is playing with fire. Most of us generally would not recommend such an activity, as we know that while fire can warm your home, it can also burn your house down. Instead, we would more likely suggest learning how to use fire responsibly—for the warming and cooking, not the burning.

Don’t Try This at Home

It’s a trade: your short-term validation for your partner’s long-term suffering.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

We could also compare cheating on your spouse with taking care of your health. Living through cancer can become the catalyst for making better decisions about how to live your life. Yet I wouldn't recommend smoking two packs a day to attempt to induce this appreciation—as it can also lead to another outcome.

It’s the same with relationships. Betrayal can become the catalyst for candid discussions about what hasn’t been working, open conversations about intimacy, and a renewed appreciation of what you have. Alternatively, it can lead to the loss of the relationship—the scorched-house equivalent of playing with fire.

After infidelity, both people become aware that the other person was willing to take this risk. All the post-cheating epiphanies do not erase this awareness, and it feels extremely painful and difficult to assimilate for the person who was betrayed.

Why is this? Cheating is the ultimate form of narcissistic validation. It’s a trade: your short-term validation for your partner’s long-term suffering.

And suffer they will. “I will regret it for the rest of my life,” shares one woman in a recent survey. “My marriage was already falling apart, but I will never forget the look of hurt on my now ex-husband's face when he found out. He forgave me many years ago, but I still struggle to forgive myself some twenty-plus years later.”

The Problem With Betrayal

To understand the problem with betraying your intimate partner, consider the words of Afghan-American novelist Khaled Hosseini. “There is only one sin, only one, and that is theft. Every other sin is a variation of theft,” shares Hosseini in The Kite Runner. “When you kill a man, you steal a life. You steal his wife’s right of a husband, you rob his children of a father. When you lie you steal someone’s right to truth. When you cheat, you steal the right to fairness.”

To make matters worse, when you betray another human being, it’s not just the right to fairness you are taking from them. You also take their right to believe in love, in acceptance, in belonging.

In other words, you take everything that most matters to them. “There is no more wretched act than stealing,” Hosseini concludes.

Trust in a relationship is like air. You don’t think about air unless you don’t have it.
Source: Tony Frost / Unsplash

“At the end of the day, it wasn’t the cheating that hurt the most,” confides another woman, “it was the betrayal. Someone I trusted so much didn't trust me enough to simply say, ‘Hey, I'm unhappy, and I want out.’”

Despite the harm we do to others, in our fragile, volatile search for validation, many of us are capable of seeing past how infidelity will affect the other person. We often don’t see the forest when standing right in front of a tree. We don’t think about the trust that will be eroded, and almost always never fully recaptured, if we cheat.

Why? Trust in a relationship is like air. You don’t think about air unless you don’t have it. Then it becomes the only thing you think about.

Honoring What Is Sacred

When you convince another human being to build their life around you and then take that safety and security from them through betrayal, you dispel the closest approximation to sacredness you will ever experience in your life.

It is at this point that you learn that when you destroy what is sacred, you destroy the sacred within you.

Cheating, then, is not only an ethically flawed form of validation; it also injures ourselves. We need to find better ways to express our relationship dissatisfaction.

If your partner is unable to listen to you or adapt with you for a protracted period, separation may be a recourse. It’s very simple: If you can’t continue your commitment, tell them rather than going down the road of pretend. They deserve as much from you.

Once you’ve come clean, you can move in another direction in your intimate life—and seek the Holy Grail of external validation you’ve been craving—knowing you were honest and did what you could to preserve the sacred within your relationship.

item.title: You Have No Idea What I'm Thinking
item.description:
Theory of Mind

You Have No Idea What I'm Thinking

Theory of mind explains how we guess what others think—and often get it wrong.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Theory of mind refers to the act of modeling others' thoughts, without knowing what they actually think.
  • Theory of mind influences relationships, communication, and political disagreements.
  • A little less certainty and a little more curiosity can help everyone understand each other.

I woke to the sound of my boyfriend getting out of bed, and my heart started racing. This is it, I thought. We’re getting engaged. We were in the Bahamas and had been dating for a few years. He had set an alarm so we could watch the sunrise, which was very out of character. He got up to brush his teeth, which added evidence to my theory.

As he brushed, I tried to make myself look effortlessly beautiful by raking my fingers through my hair. When he came in to “wake me up,” I smiled and followed him doe-eyed to the balcony, where we watched the sunrise. Any minute now, I thought. Any minute. But the minutes ticked by; he seemed relaxed and not at all ready to ask a life-changing question.

Finally, when the sun was up, he announced he was going back to bed. I said I was going to stay on the balcony a few more minutes so I could collect myself, put my face back together, and not come off as a psycho girlfriend.

We did eventually get married and now have two wonderful children. Communicating is one of our strong points; however, on that day, I had no idea what was going on in his mind, and he had no idea what was going on in mine.

What Is Theory of Mind?

Theory of mind (ToM) is our ability to recognize that other people have their own thoughts, feelings, beliefs, knowledge, and intentions, and to use that understanding to make sense of their behavior. The name “theory of mind” can sound unapproachable, like an overly academic topic that belongs in scientific journals rather than dinner-table conversation; however, I’d argue it’s a basic foundation of sophisticated human communication, and deserves its time to shine.

You may not have heard the term theory of mind, but you're probably familiar with related ideas: perspective-taking, putting yourself in someone else's shoes, reading the room, empathy, social awareness, emotional intelligence, and people skills. All of these have something in common: ToM. But why is it called a "theory"? Because humans behave like amateur scientists all day, subconsciously creating models of what others are thinking and feeling, collecting data, and adapting their beliefs based on new evidence. We can’t crack open someone’s skull, so we create a theory of what is in their mind. On the day I didn’t get engaged, my theory of my husband’s mind was that he was planning to propose, and I had collected data to support it. His theory of my mind was that I’d really enjoy the sunrise.

Studying Theory of Mind

I was introduced to theory of mind in 2012 while studying speech-language pathology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. I was focused on children with hearing loss, and I learned how differences in access to everyday language and conversation can shape how kids with hearing loss understand others’ thoughts and beliefs. The research hooked me immediately. I began devouring everything I could find on the subject, eventually designing full-day workshops for educators and clinicians and presenting them across the country and internationally.

The more time I spent teaching these workshops, the more I started seeing theory of mind everywhere: in misunderstandings with friends, arguments with my husband, and encounters with strangers whose behavior baffled me. My undergraduate degree was in political science, so I also became fascinated by how confidently we assign motives to people on the other side of a political debate. We decide they are uninformed, selfish, or gullible, often without knowing anything about their lives or the rationale for their belief. I began wondering whether recognizing the limits of our own assumptions might make us a little more curious about how someone else arrived at theirs.

Before long, my reading spilled into research on autism, humor, deception, marriage, mental illness, and prejudice. What started as a specialized clinical interest turned into a lens for understanding almost every kind of human interaction. At the same time, I grew increasingly surprised that such a useful concept remained so invisible to the public. I read a lot of popular psychology books. A lot. I cannot tell you how many times I have found myself wanting to scream into the pages, "You're talking about theory of mind! It's all theory of mind! Just call it what it is!" Well, maybe not all of it, but it hides under far more of our daily lives than we realize.

More than anything, I hope to make a case for something we could all use a little more of: intellectual humility. My goal is not to prevent every misunderstanding, or to convince you to agree with everyone you meet. It is simply to help us notice the gap between what we actually know about another person and what we have decided must be true. That awareness can change what we do in a tense moment. Are we working with different information? Do we understand each other perfectly and simply want different things? Have I spent the last 20 minutes planning a wedding without just cause? We could all benefit from a little less certainty and a little more curiosity.

item.title: Why AI Failures Capture Our Attention
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why AI Failures Capture Our Attention

Risk salience can distort how we evaluate new technologies.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Salient risks can overshadow equally important risks that receive less attention.
  • Vivid AI failures are easier to recall, making them seem more common than they are.
  • Familiar risks often fade into the background, distorting comparisons with new technologies.
Source: AI-generated with ChatGPT 5.5

A while back, Paul Bloom wrote about the death of Kit Kat, a beloved San Francisco cat struck by a Waymo taxi. His broader point wasn't really about Kit Kat, though. He used that story as a springboard to discuss how we evaluate new technologies. His argument was essentially that we often judge a new technology by whether it ever fails rather than by how it compares with the technology or practices it might replace.

That creates an impossibly high standard. Failures are going to occur, whether we're talking about new technologies or the people and practices they might replace. The relevant question is how frequently those failures occur relative to the available alternatives. But Bloom's essay got me thinking about a slightly different question: Why are we so naturally drawn to evaluating new technologies against such an unrealistic standard?

Risk vs. Risk Salience

Every decision we make involves weighing costs, benefits, and risks, whether consciously or otherwise. And while that sounds straightforward enough, there are a few important points worth making. The biggest of these is that there's a difference between actual risk and perceived risk. Actual risk refers to the objective likelihood that something bad will happen. Perceived risk reflects how risky we believe that outcome to be, regardless of whether our assessment is accurate. Of course, the two don't always align, and that's really not a surprise.[1]

One reason for that is that some risks become much more salient than others. Risk salience reflects how much attention we devote to a particular risk at a given moment. When a risk becomes especially salient, it tends to occupy a disproportionate amount of our attention, increasing the weight we assign to it when making decisions.

I'll use commercial air travel to help explain. Fatal airplane crashes are extraordinarily rare, yet they receive extensive media coverage and often dominate the news cycle for days. As a result, many people become temporarily more anxious about flying, even though the actual risk has changed little, if at all. As the story fades from the headlines, so does the salience of that particular risk. While the objective danger remains largely the same, our perception of it often doesn’t.

Of course, there's a good reason our minds work this way. From an evolutionary standpoint, paying attention to newly emerging or highly apparent threats is often adaptive. A rustle in the bushes, an unfamiliar predator, or a recently contaminated food source may deserve immediate attention, even before we have precise information about the actual level of danger. A tendency to rapidly shift attention toward potential threats can improve survival, even if it occasionally leads us to overestimate their likelihood.

But this tendency becomes less helpful when we're deciding between competing alternatives. Those decisions require us to weigh multiple costs, benefits, and risks simultaneously. When one risk becomes especially salient, it can crowd out consideration of the others, distorting the comparison.

Risk Salience and the Availability Heuristic

One reason some risks exert such a strong influence on our decisions is the availability heuristic.[2] Rather than calculating probabilities every time we face a decision, we often rely on a mental shortcut: The easier it is to recall examples of something happening, the more likely we assume it’ll occur again. In everyday situations, it serves us reasonably well. Events that happen frequently are often easier to remember simply because we encounter them more often.

The relationship isn't perfect, though. Some events become highly memorable because they’re emotionally charged, unusual, or receive extensive media attention. A commercial airplane crash, a shark attack, or a widely publicized crime may remain vivid in our minds. Their memorability can make them feel more common than they actually are, increasing the weight we assign to those risks when making future decisions.

This is one reason highly publicized artificial intelligence (AI) failures can have such a powerful influence on public opinion. A tragic story involving an AI companion, a driverless car, or an incorrect AI-generated medical recommendation is memorable precisely because they're emotionally compelling. And while those stories deserve attention, that attention makes them unusually easy to retrieve from memory. This can increase the weight we assign to the associated risks, making them feel more common than they may actually be.

Now, this doesn't mean the risks themselves are unimportant or imaginary. Sometimes a widely publicized failure reveals a genuine problem requiring immediate attention. As those memorable examples accumulate in our minds, though, the associated risks often begin to occupy more space in our thinking than less memorable, but potentially more common, risks. And that sets the stage for another subtle judgment shift. Familiar risks associated with the status quo begin to fade into the background.

Risks We Stop Noticing

The availability heuristic helps explain why certain risks receive disproportionate attention, but it doesn't fully explain why we sometimes evaluate new technologies against an unrealistically high standard. To understand that, we also need to consider the role of the status quo.

Once a technology becomes familiar, many of its risks gradually fade into the background. They don't disappear, of course. We simply stop devoting much conscious attention to them. When driving, most of us buckle our seat belts, check our mirrors, and navigate traffic with little conscious thought about the possibility of a serious accident. The risks remain real, but they’ve become part of the background of everyday life.

The same thing happens across countless domains. Physicians sometimes make diagnostic mistakes. Human drivers become distracted, impaired, or fatigued. These risks are well documented, but because they’re familiar, they don't often dominate our thinking in the way a novel AI failure might.[3]

As such, we often don't evaluate a new technology and the status quo under the same psychological conditions. One side is evaluated under a spotlight, the other under ordinary lighting. Familiarity changes which risks command our attention, with our focus often on newer, more visible risks.

Restoring an Appropriate Comparison

This is not to suggest that we should ignore highly publicized failures. Sometimes they reveal genuine problems requiring immediate attention. A widely publicized AI failure may expose a design flaw, identify an unforeseen risk, or demonstrate a technology isn't yet ready for widespread adoption. So, while salient risks deserve investigation, they shouldn't become the entire basis for our evaluation.

This brings me back to Bloom's original point. When deciding whether a new technology should be adopted, restricted, or abandoned, whether it ever fails isn’t the right question. Almost every technology does. Instead, we should be more focused on whether the technology performs better or worse than the alternatives available to us.

So, the next time a dramatic story about AI captures your attention, consider whether its salience is influencing your judgment. Rather than evaluating the failure in isolation, ask how the costs, benefits, and risks of the new technology compare with those of the available alternatives.
