item.title: Parents, Before You Buy GTA VI for Your Kids, Read This
item.description:
Video Game Addiction

Parents, Before You Buy GTA VI for Your Kids, Read This

Personal Perspective: Stealing cars is the least concerning thing about the new "must have" game.

Posted November 23, 2026

Fifteen years ago, I wrote an article about the Grand Theft Auto (GTA) franchise and its impact on underage boys who played it.1 For the uninitiated, GTA is a series of single player, action-adventure games designed for adults which has just released version six after a lull of 13 years. In 2011, when I wrote that article, I worked in a child and adolescent mental health service (CAMHS) where I saw countless referrals for boys aged nine to 13 whose behaviour was concerning, whose emotions were dysregulated and whose spare time was spent playing GTA.

They played for several hours a day, behind closed doors, with their parents’ consent. I heard about the boys’ inability to concentrate, their uncontrollability, their use of sexually explicit language, their violence towards siblings and peers and their lack of empathy. In GTA, violence is commonplace and the role of female characters is merely to provide visual and sexual gratification. I wondered about the link between the boys’ gaming and what adults around them were witnessing.

I was particularly concerned by the sexual violence in games like GTA and its impact on sexually developing boys. In GTA IV,2 the protagonist picks up prostitutes, drives them to secluded locations and selects from three levels of service — masturbation, fellatio or full intercourse — while listening to a sexually explicit audio. Afterwards, they choose whether to pay the women or kill them. An early scene in GTA V3 shows sex with a woman on a kitchen counter. Players also visit strip clubs, where they watch, flirt with and fondle female dancers. GTA V also contained a coded minigame described as (even more) “interactive and sexually explicit” which led to its reclassification in the US from M (mature) to AO (adult only).

I’ve heard the argument touted vociferously that there is no link between sexually explicit and violent gaming and sexually explicit and violent language and behaviour. I’ve read plenty of research to the contrary, especially relating to young people whose brains and behaviours are shaped by these and all early experiences. As with most things, context is paramount. Many of the boys I worked with in CAMHS grew up in families where boundaries were fragile at best. Their parents had, after all, sanctioned games which allowed them to simulate sex and violence. Many homes featured domestic abuse and/or trauma and neglect. In order to escape their miserable realities, these children retreated into fantasy worlds of gaming, where they formed identifications with killers, cannibals and abusers of women. Holding a gun in their (virtual) hand while a (virtual) female companion provided sexual gratification, they could press pause on their own intolerable vulnerability and feel omnipotent, while the chaos around them ensued. I remember the chilling response from one ten-year-old when I asked what he liked about the games and he told me, “Swearing and killing whores”. I wonder how your son would answer that question. Maybe ask him.

And so, to GTA VI, the long-awaited, highly anticipated addition to the $10 billion dollar franchise, which many boys bunked off school to play on the day of its release and many more added to their Christmas list. Of course, it’s more explicit. Of course, the graphics are more realistic. Of course there’s more extreme content. We’re told that high impact violence is “less restrained” than in previous versions and now includes dismemberment and decapitation. Like that’s a selling point. Sex is no longer “implied” or “off camera” but is unequivocally explicit. There’s a mission set in a pornographer’s mansion, a corseted woman hitting golf balls at a man’s testicles and the familiar strip clubs where players can rub the dancer’s breasts and buttocks while inhaling cocaine. Parents are feverishly and obliviously “adding to basket”.

This is the blatant stuff, but there’s also subliminal messaging which the creators describe as “satirical political parody”. This includes an anti-transgender billboard and a “no paws clause” to keep the state “free of furries”. There are political insults and racial slurs, including reference to the N-word. These are supposedly digs at right wing rhetoric, but I doubt your kid will get the irony.

GTA VI introduces the first female protagonist, demonstrating that women can be as “violent, tough and deeply messed up as the men.”5 And in another move to redress the gender imbalance, male strippers have been recruited to the clubs. An avid fan of GTA described GTA VI as: “absurdly foul-mouthed, filthy and over-the-top offensive in every imaginable way. It does not so much push the boundaries of taste as ignore the existence of taste. It contains every perverted scenario you could imagine.”5 GTA is classified globally as 18+, Mature or Adult Only. As one reviewer stated, “I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating.”5

I’m no prude. I regularly and willingly talk about sex, fetish, drugs and alcohol with young people, if that’s what’s on their mind. I’m often the one advocating for leniency and compromise regarding arbitrary age limits. But I am not on board with parents sanctioning their teens and pre-teens simulating dismemberment and decapitation, sex with prostitutes, killing sex workers and sexually harassing female dancers, while picking up “satirical” discriminatory language about gender, sexual and ethnic diversity. So please, for their sake, and the sake of everyone they are yet to meet, don’t buy GTA VI for your children.

item.title: How to Get What You Really Want
item.description:
Career

How to Get What You Really Want

Sometimes, letting go of an outcome helps us discover what truly matters.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Focus is a double-edged sword. Obsessive attachment to an outcome can become counterproductive.
  • We sometimes mistake a proxy for the goal itself. Reflection allows us to reconsider what we want.
  • Letting go doesn't mean giving up. It means loosening our attachment to a particular outcome.

I've played tennis all my life, first in school and now recreationally in adult leagues. I've had my wins and losses. Recently, I looked up my computer records—my cumulative record over the last 20 years. A 0.500 win-loss percentage! Couldn't be more perfect.

Years ago, I heard a line in a commercial: "If only I didn't have to work, I could have been a pro!"

I laughed out loud. The irony, of course, is that you have to work precisely because you're not good enough to be a pro!

Even though I rationally knew that my weekend matches didn't matter all that much, when I was younger, I wanted to win so badly! I would have given anything if somebody had told me the secret to winning.

How can I win this game?
Source: AI-Generated

So here it is. The secret.

The Paradox of Wanting

What I didn't understand in my youth, being goal-driven and perhaps a bit intense, was that while commitment and engagement are critical to achieving our goals, obsessive attachment to a particular outcome can sometimes be counterproductive, preventing us from getting closer to what we want so badly.

One of the brain's remarkable strengths is its ability to focus, learn, and adapt. Sustained attention and practice allow us to develop specialized skills, whether playing the guitar, shooting a basketball, or designing a bridge.

I wrote in a previous post that we become what we attend to. But focus has an opportunity cost. The more intensely we attend to one thing, the less we notice everything else.

I now realize that what my younger self really wanted was to become a better tennis player. Winning had become a proxy for that larger goal. Over time, however, I began to mistake the proxy for the goal itself.

This isn't advice to say that winning doesn't matter and we should just chill out. It's perfectly fine to want to win and be fiercely competitive on the court. But once I realized that I had become overly attached to winning as proof that I was a good tennis player, I was able to loosen my grip on the outcome.

Sure, I still don't like to lose. But by reflecting on what I love about the game—learning and expressing different skills through my body and enjoying time with like-minded players—I've become better able to learn from my losses and mistakes, and to be genuinely in awe of my opponents' amazing plays.

Creating Space to Choose

Dancing on the dance floor and losing yourself in the moment can be exhilarating. But sometimes, stepping onto the balcony allows you to reflect and see the larger picture.

Of course, reflecting is easier said than done, especially when something genuinely matters to us. Not getting a promotion genuinely hurts. It's also OK to leave the dance floor for a while and get a change of scenery. Going on vacation, spending time with family, or removing ourselves from the situation may create some space.

And when we come back, we may have renewed interest in getting that promotion next time around. We can recommit ourselves to work and perhaps make an effort to seek feedback from our colleagues. Or we may realize that we've been sacrificing so much for work and that the promotion was a proxy for the recognition we craved. We may then decide to change course by setting new boundaries or pivoting to a different line of work.

Letting go does not mean that we stop caring or trying. It means loosening our attachment to a particular outcome. We can still want something deeply without letting that desire define us.

And when we let it go a bit, curious things may happen. We may relax, become more open to other possibilities, or feel more comfortable in our own skin. Sometimes, this even helps us achieve what we originally wanted. But that isn't the point—or a guarantee.

The word "freedom" keeps circling back in my mind here: the ability to choose and re-commit to a goal worth pursuing. This freedom does not necessarily weaken our commitment, but it makes our commitment more meaningful.

A Richer Understanding of Success

Of course, if someone had told my younger self to stop caring so much about winning, I probably wouldn't have listened. I might even have been annoyed. Sometimes, we have to learn these things through our own disappointments.

Would my younger self have considered a 0.500 winning record after 20 years a success? Hard to say. But along the way, I made many friends, experienced the ups and downs of competition, and learned not only new skills but also something about myself.

The numbers may not show it, but I would consider that a success.

Sometimes, years later, you get what you once wanted so badly.

Sometimes, you realize that what you want has changed.

item.title: Do You Have a Work Spouse? Here's What Research Says
item.description:
Career

Do You Have a Work Spouse? Here's What Research Says

What makes some workplace friendships different from the rest.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Work spouses are close, platonic colleagues who share trust, support, and mutual respect.
  • Work spouses can offer accountability, motivation, and support for shared professional goals.
  • These friendships can make work more enjoyable and provide valuable emotional and practical support.

Last week, I found myself running against one of my closest friends for an elected leadership position in a professional organization.

When it was my turn to introduce myself, I blurted out that my opponent was my "work spouse" and that I would be absolutely thrilled if they won. And I meant it (although they may have wished I'd not introduced them in that way).

The two of us collaborate on research, are currently co-editing a book, and have developed a friendship that extends well beyond our professional responsibilities. We celebrate each other's accomplishments, offer advice, and understand the sometimes ridiculous aspects of academia that can be difficult to explain to anyone outside it.

Just as I was about to post a selfie of us on Instagram with a quick little caption about appreciating my work spouse, I remembered that my dear friend, the late Dr. Chad McBride, had actually published research on this very topic. So, naturally, I decided to blog about it instead.

My colleague Dr. Dawn Braithwaite has also written about this research, highlighting the emotional support, trust, and sense of connection that work-spouse relationships can provide. I think these relationships can also shape how we approach our work, develop professionally, and navigate the challenges of our careers.

What Exactly Is a Work Spouse?

You've probably heard someone refer to a colleague as their "work wife" or "work husband." Maybe you've even used the term yourself. But what makes someone a work spouse rather than simply a friend or colleague at work?

In 2015, communication scholars M. Chad McBride and Karla Mason Bergen examined how people characterized their work-spouse relationships. Analyzing responses from 269 participants, they identified recurring characteristics, including trust, honesty, loyalty, respect, emotional connection, and mutual support.

Based on these findings, they defined work spouses as close, platonic workplace friends who share a strong emotional connection and provide support for one another. Despite the marital terminology, these relationships are generally understood as nonromantic and nonsexual.

I've always found the term particularly interesting because my parents are both actual spouses and work spouses. They're professors in the same discipline, and I grew up watching them navigate their personal and professional lives together. So when I call my friend my work spouse, I'm describing something quite different from the relationship I've watched my parents share. Still, both relationships involve professional collaboration, mutual support, and an understanding of each other's work.

Why Do These Relationships Develop?

Think about how much of our lives we spend working. We navigate stressful deadlines, celebrate accomplishments, complain about frustrating policies, and occasionally wonder why we chose our particular professions in the first place. Naturally, we develop relationships with the people experiencing those things alongside us.

And sometimes, those relationships become particularly meaningful because our co-workers understand things about our professional lives that people outside our workplaces might not.

For instance, my work spouse understands why I might be nervous to present a new idea, excited by a revise and resubmit, or frustrated about a particular obligation. I don't have to spend time explaining the context before getting to the actual story, and sometimes that can be really nice.

But it's more than having someone who understands your workplace. Sometimes, that person is also helping you get the work done.

The two of us work on projects together, but we also spend time working independently alongside one another. We bounce ideas off each other, provide feedback, and hold each other accountable for making progress. I find that I'm often more productive when we're working together, even when we're tackling entirely different tasks.

These experiences are reflected in McBride and Bergen's findings. Participants described work spouses as people they could confide in, seek advice from, and rely on during stressful periods. Others talked about having someone who motivated them, challenged them professionally, or simply made difficult workdays more enjoyable.

And I imagine these experiences aren't unique to academia. Think about teachers planning lessons together, nurses navigating difficult shifts, or colleagues working toward a shared deadline.

Dr. Braithwaite has also highlighted how work spouses provide an important source of emotional support, helping people feel understood, valued, and connected to their workplaces. I think there's another dimension worth considering: these relationships can also influence how we actually do our work. Beyond having someone to confide in, a work spouse might be someone who challenges our ideas, helps us stay accountable, and makes us better at what we do.

When Work and Friendship Overlap

Of course, mixing friendship and work isn't always straightforward. Management scholars Whitman and Mandeville (2021) explored how work-spouse relationships blur the boundaries between our professional and personal lives, including potential complications involving favoritism, romantic partners, and competing responsibilities.

But I think sometimes, the challenges are simply those that come with being close friends who also work together.

My work spouse and I have certainly had our rough patches. We've had to figure out how to support each other as friends while also being honest and productive collaborators. We've had plenty of conversations about what we need from one another, including when one of us needs encouragement and when one of us needs to be told we're being unreasonable and need to chill out.

This is something McBride and his colleagues explored further. In two subsequent studies, McBride, Thorson, and Bergen (2020a, 2020b) examined how work spouses manage privacy and navigate one another's feelings and professional identities. Their research illustrates that even close workplace friendships involve decisions about what to share, when to speak up, and how to support one another.

As Dr. Braithwaite has noted, healthy work-spouse relationships can help us feel more understood, valued, and connected to our careers. Sometimes, the people who understand us best professionally are also the people who become our closest friends. They celebrate our accomplishments, challenge us when we need it, help us navigate difficult situations, and sometimes make the work itself a little more enjoyable.

Maybe that's what makes a work spouse special -- it's more than having a friend at work, but it's also having someone who makes the work, and perhaps even the person doing the work, a little better.

item.title: 5 Ways to Feel Happier Today
item.description:
Oxytocin

5 Ways to Feel Happier Today

Boost your brain’s feel-good chemistry.

Posted November 23, 2026

Key points
  • Novelty can stimulate the release of dopamine, a chemical involved in motivation and reward.
  • Positive social interactions can engage your brain's reward systems.
  • An instant happiness boost can come from sunshine.
Source: Soloviova Liudmyla/Shutterstock

Your body and brain work together to shape how you feel. Although happiness is influenced by many factors, certain brain chemicals play important roles in pleasure, motivation, connection, and well-being. Four of these are dopamine, serotonin, oxytocin, and endorphins.

Here are five healthy actions you can take today that can trigger the brain's feel-good chemistry and help you feel happier:

1. Do Something New

Doing something new engages your mind in an entirely different way from how it works when you’re doing the same old activities day after day. Your brain loves a challenge.

When you’re feeling low, pick something you’ve never done before that sounds like fun, and give it a go. Bake a cake. Take a yoga class. Go on a hike. Put up a tent—and then sleep in it. Create a work of art. Do a headstand. Rearrange your room.

Novelty can stimulate the release of dopamine, a chemical involved in motivation and reward, which may be one reason new experiences feel energizing. It doesn’t even matter if you aren’t successful (like if your cake comes out salty or your tent collapses). The happiness may even come from getting out of your comfort zone.

2. Do Something Kind

One of the easiest shortcuts to feeling happier is helping someone else feel good. Give a genuine and unexpected compliment. Shovel snow off a neighbor’s sidewalk without being asked. Help an elderly person across the street or set up their cellphone. Plan a meal for your family and prepare it. Say thank you, sincerely and often.

When you do something kind for another person, you strengthen your connection with them. Such positive social interactions can engage your brain's reward systems, including those involving dopamine, and may also involve oxytocin, which plays an important role in social bonding.

Helping someone else can therefore feel good for both of you.

3. Get a Hug

When two people shake hands or share a welcomed hug, a connection is made that’s more than skin-deep. In each of their brains, oxytocin can be released, which helps create a bond between them and feelings of comfort and safety.

If you don’t have anyone with whom you want to hug or hold hands at the moment, you can experience the effects of oxytocin by nuzzling a dog or petting a cat. In fact, when you cuddle your pets, their brains release oxytocin so they feel safe and happy, too.

4. Go Outside

When you step outside, your entire world changes. The light, the temperature, the sounds you hear, the colors, even the qualities of the air perk up your senses. Each of these gives your brain a boost and can improve your mood.

An instant happiness boost can come from sunshine. Natural light helps regulate your body's internal clock and can influence mood-regulating brain systems, including those involving serotonin. For some people, a light therapy lamp (not a tanning lamp) can also help, particularly during months when there is less daylight.

5. Move Your Body

Exercise has the potential to trigger many feel-good chemicals. You don’t have to be an athlete. You don’t have to take a class. You just need to find a physical outlet that feels right to your body and then make time for it.

A few possibilities: yoga; jumping jacks; a competitive or not-so-competitive sports team; hiking in beautiful places.

As an extra bonus, when you move your body, some of the chemicals that can be released are endorphins, which ease pain and stress.

Takeaway

You don't have to wait for happiness to find you. By doing new things, being kind to others, connecting with people and pets, spending time outdoors, and moving your body, you can encourage positive feelings. These activities won't make every problem disappear, but they can give you energy and better perspective to help deal with your troubles.
